items.title: Encounter the Phenomenon: How can a video you stream from a data center on another continent reach your phone through an undersea cable, and what carries the information along the cable?

body.html: Information crosses an ocean through a thin glass cable. We need to explain how the information is carried and why it does not leak out along the way.

Data are encoded as pulses of light. The light is guided by total internal reflection (TIR): the glass core has a larger index of refraction than the cladding around it, so light striking the core– cladding boundary at more than the critical angle, sin𝜃<sub>𝑐</sub>= 𝑛<sub>2</sub> / 𝑛<sub>1</sub>, is reflected completely.

A laser at the data center switches on and off very quickly, so each pulse stands for part of a digital code. The pulse zig-zags down the core, and every reflection sends back 100 % of the light. Because so little light is lost, repeaters spaced along the route only need to boost the signal occasionally. At the receiving end a detector converts the pulses back into electrical signals that your phone turns into video.

answer.html: The video is coded as pulses of light that travel inside glass fibers, trapped by total internal reflection at the core–cladding boundary, so large amounts of data cross an ocean with very little loss.

check.html: The core must have the higher index of refraction, otherwise there would be no critical angle and light would escape.

items.title: Science and Engineering Practice (Ask Questions): Write questions for the driving question board about how a streaming video crosses an ocean in a glass cable.

body.html: A good driving-board question is testable and tied to the physics of the module (reflection, refraction, indices of refraction).

answer.html: (1) Why does light stay inside a glass cable that is bent around a ship's winch? (2) What would happen to the signal if the cladding had the same index of refraction as the core? (3) How fast does light travel in the glass compared with in air, and how long does a signal take to cross the ocean? (4) How does a pulse of light represent a 0 or a 1? (5) Why do the signals need boosting every so often?

items.title: CER: Module 16, Make Your Claim: Make a claim that answers "How can a video stream cross an ocean through an undersea cable?" and say what evidence you would need.

body.html: A CER claim must answer the question, be supported by evidence, and be tied to a scientific principle.

answer.html: A streamed video crosses the ocean as pulses of light in glass fibers, and total internal reflection at the core–cladding boundary keeps the light inside the fiber. Evidence to collect in the module: the relation 𝑛= 𝑐/ 𝑣, Snell's law, the critical-angle equation sin𝜃<sub>𝑐</sub>= 𝑛<sub>2</sub> / 𝑛<sub>1</sub>, and measurements showing that the core has the larger index of refraction.

items.title: Lesson 1, Focus Question: Why does a wet road at night show a clear mirror-like image of the streetlights, while a dry road does not?

body.html: Every ray obeys the law of reflection, 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>. What differs between surfaces is how smooth they are compared with the wavelength of light.

Wet pavement is covered by a thin, flat film of water, which is smooth. Rays from one streetlight reach it in a bundle, and they leave in a bundle that still appears to diverge from one point, so your eye sees an image of the lamp (specular reflection). Dry asphalt is rough on the scale of a wavelength, so its surface normals point in many directions. Rays from the same lamp leave in many directions (diffuse reflection) and no image forms.

answer.html: The water film makes the road smooth, so it reflects light specularly and forms an image of the lamps; dry asphalt reflects diffusely and scatters the rays, so no image forms.

check.html: Each individual ray still obeys 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub> on the dry road; it is the many normal directions that scramble the rays.

items.title: Lesson 1, Figure 5 prompt: A cat sits on a table lit only by a lamp across the room. A wall mirror hangs beside the table. Describe how the cat is illuminated and how you see it both directly and in the mirror.

body.html: The cat is not a source of light. It must be lit by a source and then seen by diffuse reflection.

answer.html: The lamp's light strikes the cat directly (and some also reaches it after bouncing off the walls). The cat's fur scatters that light diffusely in all directions. Some scattered rays go straight to your eye, so you see the cat directly. Other scattered rays reach the mirror, which reflects them specularly, so your eye also sees an image of the cat that appears to be behind the mirror.

items.title: Lesson 1, Figure 7 prompt: The tip of a pencil is 0.80 m in front of a plane mirror. Using two rays and congruent triangles, explain why its image is 0.80 m behind the mirror ( 𝑥𝑖= −𝑥𝑜).

body.html: 𝑥<sub>𝑜</sub>= 0.80 m. Show that the image distance has the same size and is behind the mirror.
The law of reflection plus congruent right triangles.

Ray 1 travels from the pencil tip along the normal, hits the mirror at 0°, and reflects straight back. Ray 2 hits the mirror at some other point with 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>. Extending both reflected rays backward gives sight lines that meet at the image point. The right triangle formed by the object, the foot of the normal, and the point where ray 2 strikes, and the matching triangle on the other side of the mirror share a side along the mirror, both have a right angle at the foot of the normal, and have equal angles at the strike point (because 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>). They are congruent, so the image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

answer.html: The triangles are congruent, so |𝑥<sub>𝑖</sub>| = 𝑥<sub>𝑜</sub>= 0.80 m. The image is behind the mirror (virtual), so 𝑥<sub>𝑖</sub>= −0.80 m.

check.html: The pencil and its image are 1.60 m apart, twice the distance from pencil to mirror.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It?: A 1.70-m-tall person stands 2.5 m from a plane mirror. Describe the image: its type, orientation, height, position, and how far it is from the person.

body.html: ℎ<sub>𝑜</sub>= 1.70 m, 𝑥<sub>𝑜</sub>= 2.5 m.
A plane mirror gives a virtual, upright, same-size image with 𝑥<sub>𝑖</sub>= −𝑥<sub>𝑜</sub> and ℎ<sub>𝑖</sub>= ℎ<sub>𝑜</sub>.
𝑥<sub>𝑖</sub>= −𝑥<sub>𝑜</sub>= −2.5 m (2.5 m behind the mirror). ℎ<sub>𝑖</sub>= ℎ<sub>𝑜</sub>= 1.70 m. The distance from the person to the image is 2.5 m + 2.5 m = 5.0 m.

answer.html: The image is virtual, upright, 1.70 m tall, located 2.5 m behind the mirror (𝑥<sub>𝑖</sub>= −2.5 m), which is 5.0 m from the person; it is also reversed front to back.

check.html: No light actually passes through the image position, which is why it is virtual.

items.title: Lesson 1, Identify Crosscutting Concepts (Investigate) and the Forensics Lab "A Little Time to Reflect": In a lab a laser reflects from a plane mirror at five angles of incidence. Build a crosscutting-concepts table for Lesson 1 and predict the results of the lab.

question.html: Identify Crosscutting Concepts: Build your own table. Examples: Patterns (the law of reflection 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub> holds for every ray); Cause and effect (surface roughness causes specular versus diffuse reflection); Structure and function (a polished, smooth surface gives a clear image); Systems and models (the ray model of light). Forensics Lab (online, data not available): The expected result is that the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, within measurement uncertainty. For the five incident angles 15°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 75°, a sample of what good data look like is below (these are sample values, not real measurements). 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub> sample 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub> 15° 15° 30° 31° 45° 45° 60° 59° 75° 75° A plot of 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub> versus 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub> is a straight line through the origin with slope ≈1.

answer.html: Expected result: 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub> (slope ≈ 1.0). The sample table above is illustrative; actual data are online and not available here.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 1: Why does a dull, matte tabletop show no reflection of a lamp, but the same table covered with clear gloss varnish does?

body.html: Reflection is specular only if the surface is smooth compared with the wavelength of light.

The matte finish has microscopic bumps, so the surface normals point in many directions and the reflection is diffuse. The varnish flows into the bumps and hardens into a smooth, flat top surface. Now parallel rays meet parallel normals and leave in parallel, so the lamp's rays keep their order and an image forms.

answer.html: The varnish fills in the microscopic roughness and makes a smooth surface, so the reflection changes from diffuse to specular.

check.html: The same idea explains why a wet sheet of paper looks shinier.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 2: A ray of light reflects from a plane mirror with an angle of reflection of 52° measured from the normal. What was its angle of incidence?

body.html: 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 52°; find 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>.
The law of reflection, 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>, with both angles measured from the normal.
𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 52°.

answer.html: 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>= 52°

check.html: Neither angle is measured from the mirror surface, so no conversion is needed.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 3: A ray strikes a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of 27°. (a) What is the angle of reflection? (b) What angle does the reflected ray make with the mirror surface? (c) What is the angle between the incident and reflected rays?

body.html: 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>= 27°.
Law of reflection. The surface is 90° from the normal, so angles with the surface are 90° minus angles from the normal.
(a) 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>= 27°. (b) The angle with the mirror surface is 90° −27° = 63°. (c) The angle between the incident and reflected rays is 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>+ 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 2(27°) = 54°.

check.html: In (b), 63° and 27° add to 90°.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 4: A laser beam strikes a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of 24°. The mirror is then turned so that the angle of incidence increases by 17°. What is the new angle of reflection?

body.html: 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub><sub>, initial</sub> = 24°; the angle of incidence increases by 17°.
Law of reflection, 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>, applied to the new angle.
New 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>= 24° + 17° = 41°, so 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>= 41°.

answer.html: 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 41°

check.html: The reflected ray turned by 2(17°) = 34° as the mirror turned by 17°, a useful fact about rotating mirrors.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 5: Two plane mirrors meet at a right angle. A ray strikes mirror 1 with an angle of incidence of 25° and then reflects to mirror 2. What is the angle of reflection from mirror 2?

body.html: 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub><sub>1</sub> = 25°; mirrors are perpendicular; find 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub><sub>2</sub>.
Law of reflection at each mirror. The normals of two perpendicular mirrors are also perpendicular, so the ray, the corner, and the two strike points form a triangle.

Off mirror 1, 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub><sub>1</sub> = 25°, so the reflected ray makes 90° −25° = 65° with the surface of mirror 1. The triangle formed by the two mirrors and the ray has angles 90° (at the corner) and 65° (at mirror 1), so the ray meets mirror 2 at 180° −90° −65° = 25° to its surface. So the ray makes 90° −25° = 65° with the normal of mirror 2.

answer.html: 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 65° at the second mirror

check.html: For perpendicular mirrors 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub><sub>1</sub> + 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub><sub>2</sub> = 90°, and 25° + 65° = 90°.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 6 (Challenge): A bicycle reflector is a corner reflector made of two plane mirrors meeting at 90°. A ray strikes the first mirror with an angle of incidence of 35°. (a) What is its angle of incidence on the second mirror? (b) Through what total angle is the direction of the ray turned by the two reflections, and what does that tell you about the outgoing ray?

body.html: 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub><sub>1</sub> = 35°, mirrors at 90°. Find 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub><sub>2</sub> and the total turning.
For two mirrors at 90° the angles of incidence add to 90° (Problem 5). A reflection at angle of incidence 𝜃 turns the ray's direction by 180° −2𝜃.

(a) 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub><sub>2</sub> = 90° −35° = 55°. (b) First bounce turns the ray by 180° −2(35°) = 110°. Second bounce turns it by 180° −2(55°) = 70°, in the same sense. Total turning: 110° + 70° = 180°. In general 360° −2(𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub><sub>1</sub> + 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub><sub>2</sub>) = 360° −180° = 180° whatever 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub><sub>1</sub> is.

answer.html: (a) 55° (b) 180°: the outgoing ray travels back parallel to the incoming ray, in the opposite direction

check.html: This is why a corner reflector sends a car's headlight beam straight back to the driver, for any incoming angle in the plane.

items.title: Lesson 1, Check Your Progress 7: A ray strikes a plane mirror at 68° to the normal. What angle does the reflected ray make with the mirror surface?

body.html: 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>= 68° from the normal, so the angle with the surface is 90° −68° = 22°.

answer.html: 22° with the mirror surface

check.html: 68° from the normal is close to the surface, so a small angle with the surface makes sense.

items.title: Lesson 1, Check Your Progress 8: A rabbit 35.0 cm tall stands 1.8 m in front of a plane mirror. Find the position and height of its image and say what type of image it is.

body.html: ℎ<sub>𝑜</sub>= 35.0 cm; 𝑥<sub>𝑜</sub>= 1.8 m.
Plane mirror: 𝑥<sub>𝑖</sub>= −𝑥<sub>𝑜</sub>, ℎ<sub>𝑖</sub>= ℎ<sub>𝑜</sub>, and the image is virtual and upright.
𝑥<sub>𝑖</sub>= −1.8 m (1.8 m behind the mirror); ℎ<sub>𝑖</sub>= ℎ<sub>𝑜</sub>= 35.0 cm (upright).

answer.html: Image position −1.8 m (1.8 m behind the mirror, so 3.6 m from the rabbit); height 35.0 cm; a virtual, upright image.

check.html: The rabbit and its image are on opposite sides of the mirror, at equal distances from it.

items.title: Lesson 1, Check Your Progress 9: A student says the law of reflection must fail for a crumpled sheet of aluminum foil because it does not make a clear image. Explain what is wrong with that thought.

answer.html: The law of reflection holds at every point of the foil: each ray makes the same angle with the local normal as its reflected ray does. The crumpled foil has many tiny flat facets whose normals point in different directions, so parallel incoming rays leave in many different directions (scatter), even though each individual ray obeys 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>. Because the rays are scrambled, no clear image forms.

items.title: Lesson 1, Check Your Progress 10: The rear window of a delivery truck is nearly upright, tilted so that its surface makes 70° with the horizontal and the window faces backward and slightly upward. Sunlight reflecting from it travels horizontally backward into the eyes of the driver of a following car. How high above the horizon is the Sun?

body.html: Window surface at 70° to the horizontal, so its normal points 20° above the horizontal (backward). The reflected ray is horizontal.
𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>, with the incident ray, normal and reflected ray in one plane, the incident and reflected rays on opposite sides of the normal.

The reflected ray (horizontal) makes 20° with the normal, so the incident ray must make 20° with the normal on the other side. The direction back toward the Sun is then 20° + 20° = 40° above the horizontal.

answer.html: The Sun is 40° above the horizon, behind the following car.

check.html: A ray from the Sun at 40° elevation traveling down toward the window meets a window normal at 20° and bounces horizontally. The angle between the sunlight and the reflected ray is 2(20°) = 40°, which matches the Sun's elevation because the reflected ray is horizontal.

items.title: Lesson 1, Check Your Progress 11: Why can everyone in a classroom read the text on a poster from different seats, but only a student in one spot sees the reflection of a lamp in a glossy window?

answer.html: The poster's paper is microscopically rough, so it scatters light in all directions (diffuse reflection). Rays from every point of the poster travel toward every seat, so wherever you sit, some scattered rays enter your eye. The glossy window reflects light specularly, so a ray from the lamp leaves in only one direction, and only a student at the right angle receives it.

items.title: Encounter the Phenomenon: How does light transmit information through a communication network?

body.html: Information is encoded in pulses of light. The light is sent down thin glass fibers, and it stays inside because of total internal reflection (TIR): the glass core has a higher index of refraction than the cladding, so light that strikes the core–cladding boundary at more than the critical angle is reflected completely.

A laser or LED turns data into on/off (or brightness-varying) pulses. Each pulse zig-zags along the fiber with nearly no loss, because every reflection is 100 % at angles above 𝜃<sub>𝑐</sub> (with sin𝜃<sub>𝑐</sub>= 𝑛<sub>2</sub> / 𝑛<sub>1</sub>). At the far end a detector turns the pulses back into electrical signals.

answer.html: Light carries information as coded pulses that are trapped in glass fibers by total internal reflection, so large amounts of data travel long distances with little loss.

check.html: This matches the Real-World Physics note in Lesson 3.

items.title: Science and Engineering Practice (Ask Questions): other questions about the phenomenon

body.html: Good driving-board questions are testable and tied to the physics of the module.

answer.html: (1) Why does light stay inside a fiber instead of leaking out? (2) How does the index of refraction of the core and cladding affect how much light is trapped? (3) How are pulses of light turned into data and back again? (4) Why can fibers carry more information than copper wire? (5) What happens if the fiber is bent too sharply?

items.title: CER: Module 16, Make Your Claim

body.html: A CER claim must answer the question, be supported by evidence, and be tied to a principle.

answer.html: Communication networks use pulses of light that travel through glass fibers; the light is kept inside the fiber by total internal reflection at the core–cladding boundary. Evidence to collect in the module: Snell's law, sin𝜃<sub>𝑐</sub>= 𝑛<sub>2</sub> / 𝑛<sub>1</sub>, and the fact that 𝑛<sub>core</sub> > 𝑛<sub>cladding</sub>.

items.title: Lesson 1, Focus Question: Why does light reflected from a mirror make an image while light reflected from a piece of paper does not?

body.html: Both surfaces obey the law of reflection for every single ray. What differs is how smooth the surface is compared with the wavelength of light.

A mirror is smooth, so rays that arrive parallel leave parallel (specular reflection). Rays that diverge from one point on an object still appear to diverge from one point after reflection, so your eye sees a point-for-point copy: an image. Paper is rough on the scale of a wavelength, so the surface normals point in many directions; parallel rays leave in many directions (diffuse reflection) and the rays from one object point do not keep a common source point.

answer.html: A mirror reflects light specularly, preserving the ray directions so that an image forms; paper reflects diffusely, scattering the rays so no image forms.

check.html: This is why you can read a page from any angle but cannot use it as a mirror.

items.title: Lesson 1, Figure 5 prompt: Describe how the woman is illuminated.

body.html: She is not a source of light; she must be lit by a source and then be seen by diffuse reflection.

answer.html: She is illuminated by the lamp near the mirror, with light striking her directly (and some of it also reaching her after reflecting from the mirror). Her skin and clothes scatter that light diffusely in all directions, so some of it reaches the mirror (which reflects it specularly to produce her image) and some reaches the camera or viewer directly.

items.title: Lesson 1, Figure 7 prompt: Explain why 𝑥𝑖= −𝑥𝑜.

body.html: Law of reflection plus congruent triangles.

Ray 1 hits the mirror at 0° and reflects back on itself. Ray 2 reflects with 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>. Extending both reflected rays backward gives sight lines that meet at I. Triangles OP<sub>1</sub>P<sub>2</sub> and IP<sub>1</sub>P<sub>2</sub> share side P<sub>1</sub>P<sub>2</sub>, both have a right angle at P<sub>1</sub>, and have equal angles at P<sub>2</sub> (because 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>). They are congruent, so IP<sub>1</sub> = OP<sub>1</sub>.

answer.html: The two triangles are congruent, so the image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front: |𝑥<sub>𝑖</sub>| = 𝑥<sub>𝑜</sub>. It is behind the mirror (virtual), so 𝑥<sub>𝑖</sub>= −𝑥<sub>𝑜</sub>.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It?: Summarize the properties of a plane-mirror image.

answer.html: The image is virtual (formed behind the mirror, where no light actually goes), upright, the same size as the object (ℎ<sub>𝑖</sub>= ℎ<sub>𝑜</sub>), the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front ( 𝑥<sub>𝑖</sub>= −𝑥<sub>𝑜</sub>), and front-to-back reversed.

items.title: Lesson 1, Identify Crosscutting Concepts (Investigate) and the Forensics Lab "A Little Time to Reflect"

question.html: Identify Crosscutting Concepts: This asks you to build your own table. Examples from this lesson: Patterns (the law of reflection 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub> holds for every ray); Cause and effect (surface roughness causes specular vs. diffuse reflection); Structure and function (smooth polished surface gives a clear image); Systems and models (ray and wave models of light). Forensics Lab (online, data not in the book): the measured angles are not given, so no numbers can be reported. The expected result is that the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, to within measurement uncertainty, so a plot of 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub> versus 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub> is a straight line with slope 1 through the origin.

answer.html: Expected result: 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub> (slope ≈ 1.0). Actual data are online and not available here.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 1: Why does ground glass change from diffuse to specular reflection if you spill water on it?

body.html: Reflection is specular only if the surface is smooth compared with the wavelength of light.

Ground glass is covered with tiny pits and bumps, so its surface normals point in many directions and the reflection is diffuse. Water fills the pits and forms a smooth, flat top surface. Now parallel rays meet parallel normals and reflect in parallel.

answer.html: The water fills in the microscopic roughness and makes a smooth surface, so the reflection becomes specular.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 2: Angle of incidence of a ray reflected at 35° to the normal

body.html: 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 35°; find 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>.
Law of reflection, 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>.

answer.html: 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>= 35°

check.html: Both angles are measured from the normal.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 3: Angle of incidence 42°

body.html: 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>= 42°.
Law of reflection; angles with the mirror are measured from the surface, which is 90° from the normal.
(a) 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>= 42°. (b) The angle with the mirror surface is 90° −42° = 48°. (c) The angle between the incident and reflected rays is 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>+ 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 2(42°) = 84°.

check.html: (b) and the 42° from the normal add to 90°.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 4: Laser at 38°, angle of incidence increases by 13°

body.html: 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub><sub>, initial</sub> = 38°; increases by 13°.
New 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>= 38° + 13° = 51°, and 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>.

answer.html: 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 51°

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 5: Two plane mirrors at right angles

body.html: Ray hits mirror 1 at 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>= 60° to the normal, reflects to mirror 2. Find the angle of reflection off mirror 2.
Law of reflection at each mirror; the normals of two perpendicular mirrors are perpendicular too.

Off mirror 1, 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 60°, so the reflected ray makes 90° −60° = 30° with mirror 1's surface. The triangle formed by the two mirrors and the ray has angles 90° (at the corner) and 30° (at mirror 1), so the ray meets mirror 2 at 180° −90° −30° = 60° to its surface. So the ray makes 90° −60° = 30° with the normal of mirror 2.

answer.html: 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 30° at the second mirror

check.html: 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub><sub>1</sub> + 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub><sub>2</sub> = 90° always for perpendicular mirrors.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 6 (Challenge): Retro-reflector angle

body.html: Use the result of Problem 5: for two mirrors at 90°, the angles of incidence on the two mirrors add to 90°. Each bounce turns the ray's direction, and we add up the turns.

With mirrors at 90° (Problem 5), the first bounce changes the ray's direction by 180° −2𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub><sub>1</sub> and the second by 180° −2𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub><sub>2</sub> in the same sense; the total is 360° −2(𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub><sub>1</sub> + 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub><sub>2</sub>) = 360° −180° = 180°, whatever 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub><sub>1</sub> is. So the outgoing ray is antiparallel to the incoming ray for any incident direction in the plane (see the right panel of the figure in Problem 5).

answer.html: 90° between the mirrors

check.html: This is the corner reflector used on bicycles and on the Moon (3-D version uses three mutually perpendicular mirrors).

items.title: Lesson 1, Check Your Progress 7: Ray at 80° to the normal

body.html: 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 80° from the normal, so the angle with the surface is 90° −80° = 10°.

items.title: Lesson 1, Check Your Progress 9: Law of reflection and diffuse reflection

answer.html: The law of reflection holds at every point of a rough surface: each ray makes the same angle with the local normal as its reflected ray does. On a microscopic scale the local normals point in different directions, so parallel incoming rays leave in different directions (scatter) even though each individual ray obeys 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>.

items.title: Lesson 1, Check Your Progress 10: Sunlight reflecting from a 45° rear window into a following driver's eyes

body.html: Window tilted 45° to the horizontal. The following driver looks horizontally forward, so the reflected ray travels horizontally backward.
The incident ray, reflected ray and normal obey 𝜃<sub>𝑖</sub>= 𝜃<sub>𝑟</sub>.

A window tilted at 45° has a normal that is 45° above the horizontal. The reflected ray (horizontal) makes 45° with this normal, so the incident ray must make 45° on the other side of the normal. That puts the incident ray 90° from the reflected ray, pointing straight down.

answer.html: The Sun must be directly overhead (high noon at the zenith); its rays then reflect horizontally off the 45° window into the following driver's eyes.

check.html: A ray traveling straight down reflects horizontally from a 45° mirror.

items.title: Lesson 1, Check Your Progress 11: Diffuse reflection lets you see an object from any angle

answer.html: An object's surface is microscopically rough, so it scatters incoming light in all directions. Rays from every point of the object therefore travel toward every possible viewing position; wherever you stand, some scattered rays enter your eye.
